DEBUGGING NOTES — VSCode Python Debugger (Deep Version)

No filler. No "uhm". Every term explained properly, like a mini-textbook. Read once, understand fully.

LECTURE 1 — BREAKPOINTS

Why debugging exists (the real problem)

Every coder eventually writes print() everywhere to check what's happening inside code. Problem: print statements clutter your clean code, you forget to remove them later, and for big programs you can't print everything — too much noise. Debugging is the professional replacement for print-spam. It lets you freeze your program mid-execution and look inside it, live, without touching a single line of code.

Core definition

Debugging = pausing your running program at a specific point, inspecting the current state of your variables, and moving forward one step at a time to understand exactly how the logic flows.

Every code editor (VS Code, PyCharm, IntelliJ, etc.) has its own debugger, but the concept is identical everywhere. Learn it once in VS Code, you can use it anywhere.

Why business logic matters (important, often skipped)

Knowing HOW to use a debugger tool means nothing if you don't know WHAT the correct output should be. Example: if you're debugging a "check leap year" function but don't know the actual leap year rule (divisible by 4, but not by 100, unless also by 400), you'll stare at correct-looking code and still not know if it's right or wrong. Debugging skill = tool skill + business/domain understanding. Both required.

Definition: Breakpoint

A breakpoint is a marker you place on a specific line of code that tells the editor: "When execution reaches here, STOP."

Think of it like a red flag on a highway — the car (your program) keeps running normally until it hits your flag, then it halts completely so you can inspect it.

How to set one: Click in the space just left of the line number, in the margin. A red dot appears.

How to remove one: Double-click the same red dot.

How many can you have: Unlimited. But don't spam them randomly — place them where you actually suspect the problem, or where you want visibility into what's happening.

Setup requirements before debugging

  • Virtual environment (venv): An isolated Python setup for your project so its packages don't mix with your system's global Python.
    • Activate it: source venv/bin/activate (Linux/Mac). Windows syntax is slightly different.
  • Python interpreter selection: VS Code needs to know WHICH Python to run your code with. Always pick your venv's interpreter, not the global one — otherwise your installed packages won't be found.

How to start debugging

Go to Run menu → "Python Debugger" → "Debug Python File." (There's also "Debug using launch.json" for more advanced/custom configs — not covered here, just basic file debugging.)

The Debug Control Panel — the 4 core buttons (memorize these)

  1. Continue

    • Definition: Run the program forward until it hits the NEXT breakpoint.
    • Use case: You have multiple breakpoints and want to jump between them without manually stepping through every single line in between.

  2. Step Over

    • Definition: Execute the current line completely, then move to the very next line — WITHOUT going inside any function that line calls.
    • Use case: You trust that function works fine and just want its result, not its internal steps.

  3. Step Into

    • Definition: If the current line calls a function, this jumps INSIDE that function so you can watch its internal logic line-by-line.
    • Use case: You suspect the bug is happening inside that specific function, so you want to see its private variables and steps.

  4. Restart

    • Definition: Kills the current debug session and starts the whole program fresh from the top.

  5. Stop

    • Definition: Ends the debugging session completely.

Live demo — what actually happens (worked example)

Code: a list input_list = [40, 30, 20, 10] gets passed to a function sum_of_list() which loops and adds everything up, returning the total.

  • Before any breakpoint hits, VS Code shows NO local/global variables — because nothing has been created in memory yet.
  • Breakpoint hits at first line → input_list variable now shows up in the Variables panel, along with its type (list), its length, and each index's value.
  • Press Continue → jumps to next breakpoint line. Notice: input_list is now already visible because it was created before.
  • Press Step Over on the function-call line → the function runs completely in the background, and a NEW variable appears: rest_sum = 100 (the returned value). You did NOT see what happened inside the function — it's a black box to you here.
  • Press Step Into on that same type of line instead → now you literally go INSIDE sum_of_list(). Notice something interesting: the same list is now called x inside the function (because that's the parameter name defined in the function signature) — this teaches you that variable names are just local labels; the actual data/memory is the same.
  • Inside the function, step line by line: sum = 0 created → then loop runs → sum updates each iteration (0 → 10 → 30 → 60 → 100) as it adds each list item.
  • Once function hits return, control jumps BACK to the exact line that called it, and now the returned value getsjjl stored in rest_sum.

Key takeaway (Lecture 1)

Breakpoint = pause marker. Step Over = skip function internals, trust the black box. Step Into = open the black box and watch it work. Continue = skip ahead to next flagged point. This combo is your entire toolkit for basic line-by-line investigation.

LECTURE 2 — WATCH PANEL

Definition: Watch Panel

The Watch Panel is a feature that lets you type ANY variable name or expression, and it will continuously show you its live value as you step through code — even if that variable isn't visible on your current line or even currently in scope logic-wise.

Think of it as building your own custom dashboard of things you personally care about, instead of scrolling through the full (sometimes huge) default Variables panel.

Why it's different from just looking at Variables panel

The default Variables panel shows EVERYTHING currently in scope. Watch panel lets you handpick and even COMPUTE new things — not just look at existing variables, but write expressions using them.

Example setup used

grades = [80, 90, 40, 30, 60]

Function calculates average of grades, then another function checks: if average >= 40 → pass, else fail.

How to add a watch expression

Type any valid Python expression into the watch box and hit enter/click it. Examples used in the video:

  • grades → shows the whole list.
  • grades[-1] → shows the LAST item in the list (index -1 in Python always means "last element," a very common Python trick).
  • total_sum / total_items → you can literally do MATH inside the watch box, combining two variables to manually get a value the code hasn't calculated yet (like manually computing average to double check the code's own math).
  • "pass" if status else "fail" → a Python conditional (ternary) expression. Reads as: "if status is True, give me the string pass, otherwise give me fail." This is a way to interpret a boolean value as human-readable text on the fly.
  • "great" if average > 90 else "okay" → same ternary pattern, custom-built to add your own judgment layer on top of raw numbers.

A "gotcha" worth remembering: Scope errors in Watch

If you watch a variable that belongs to a function, then step OUT of that function, the watch will throw a "name error" — because that variable's memory was destroyed the moment the function finished (this is called the variable going "out of scope"). This is NOT a bug in your program. It's expected behavior — local variables only exist while their function is running.

Persistence feature

Watch expressions STAY even if you stop and restart the debugger. You don't have to retype them every session — a genuine time-saver.

Real-world use case #1 — Huge nested payloads

In real jobs, you often deal with giant JSON responses/API payloads — sometimes 1000+ lines, with deeply nested objects (e.g., user_info containing dozens of fields, which itself contains more nested objects like address).

Printing or scrolling through the WHOLE payload to find one field is painful and slow. Instead, using watch, you directly type the exact path you care about:

data["user_info"]["address"]

This instantly shows you JUST that nested value, ignoring the rest of the noise. This is the single biggest practical reason Watch Panel exists — surgical precision instead of digging through haystacks.

Real-world use case #2 — Conditional monitoring inside loops

Imagine a loop running 100+ times. You don't want to manually click "Step Over" 100 times checking each iteration by eye. Instead, write a watch expression like:

"error" if grade < 40 else "go"

Now you just keep hitting Continue/Step, and your eyes only need to catch the word "error" when it appears — you don't need to mentally track every single value yourself. The video mentions this is a lightweight preview of what Conditional Breakpoints do properly (covered in a future lecture) — a breakpoint that only triggers/stops when a specific condition is true, instead of every single time.

Key takeaway (Lecture 2)

Watch Panel = your personal, live, computable inspector. Best used for (a) picking one exact field out of a huge nested data structure, and (b) building simple flags/conditions to catch specific situations inside loops without manually checking every iteration.

DEBUGGING NOTES — LECTURE 3: CALL STACK (Deep Version)

Same style. No filler. Every term explained fully.

What we've covered so far (quick recap mentioned in video)

  • How to inspect variables while debugging (Lecture 1).
  • How to use Watch panel to monitor expressions live (Lecture 2).
  • Now moving to: Call Stack.

Definition: Call Stack

The Call Stack is basically a recorded PATH your code has traveled through to reach the exact line you're currently paused at. It shows you the full chain of function calls — which function called which function, in order — like a ladder or trail of breadcrumbs.

Think of it like this: if Function A calls Function B, and Function B calls Function C, and you're currently stuck inside Function C — the Call Stack shows you all three: A → B → C. It answers the question "how did I even get here?"

Why the name "Stack"?

A stack is a data structure that works on a simple principle: Last In, First Out (LIFO). Imagine a pile of plates — you put a new plate on TOP, and when you remove one, you also remove from the TOP first (the most recently added one). You can't grab a plate from the middle without removing the ones above it first.

This is exactly how function calls behave in programming:

  • When a function is called → a new "frame" (a record of that function's current state — its variables, its current line) gets pushed (added) on top of the stack.
  • When that function finishes executing and returns → its frame gets popped (removed) from the top of the stack, and control goes back to whatever called it.

So the Call Stack panel in VS Code is literally showing you this live stack, frame by frame, top to bottom.

Worked example from the video

The code structure

final_price → calls → checkout()
checkout() → calculates discounted_price → calls → apply_discount()
apply_discount() → contains the actual business logic

So there are 3 levels of function calls happening, nested inside each other, one triggering the next.

Step-by-step walkthrough of what happens in the Call Stack panel

Step 1: Add a breakpoint at the very first line (final_price call). Start the debugger.

  • At this point, Call Stack panel shows only ONE entry: the file itself (e.g., lecture3_callstack.py) — because nothing else has been called yet. You're standing at ground level.

Step 2: Step Into checkout().

  • Now Call Stack panel shows TWO entries. A new frame got pushed on top: checkout() at line 7 (wherever that call sits).
  • Reading the stack top-to-bottom (or bottom-to-top depending on how it's displayed) tells you exactly: "I started at the main file, then I moved into checkout()."

Step 3: Step Into apply_discount() (called from inside checkout).

  • Now Call Stack panel shows THREE entries. Another frame pushed on top.
  • Full path visible now: main file → checkout() → apply_discount().
  • This is the real power of Call Stack — you can literally SEE the exact route your program took, function by function, to land exactly where you currently are. In a deeply nested codebase, this saves you from getting lost.

Step 4: Now reverse the process using Step Out.

  • Step Out = a debugger action that finishes the CURRENT function completely and pops you back up to whoever called it (opposite direction of Step Into).
  • Press Step Out once → apply_discount() frame gets POPPED off the top of the stack (it's done, finished, removed). You're back inside checkout().
  • Press Step Out again → checkout() frame also gets popped off. You're back at the very first/main level — only ONE frame left in the stack, same as where you started.
  • Stop the debugger entirely → the whole stack clears, nothing left.

New term introduced: Step Out

Step Out = runs the rest of the current function to completion, then jumps you back to the line right after wherever this function was originally called from — essentially popping you back UP one level in the call stack, opposite direction of Step Into (which pushes you DOWN one level).

Quick comparison table so it sticks:

Action Direction What it does
Step Into Goes DOWN (deeper) Enters a function call to see what's inside it — pushes new frame
Step Out Goes UP (shallower) Finishes current function, returns to caller — pops current frame
Step Over Stays SAME level Runs current line/function as black box, moves to next line — no frame change visible to you
Continue Jumps FORWARD Runs until next breakpoint, regardless of depth

Why Call Stack actually matters (real use case)

When you're debugging deep or nested logic — meaning function calling function calling function, several layers deep (very common in real production codebases, not just toy examples) — it's extremely easy to get lost and forget "wait, how did I even end up inside this function? Who called this?"

The Call Stack panel eliminates that confusion completely. At ANY point during debugging, you can just glance at it and instantly know:

  1. Which function you're currently inside.
  2. The EXACT chain of functions that led you here, in order.
  3. What each function in that chain was doing (since VS Code lets you click on any frame in the stack to jump back and inspect that function's own local variables at that point in time — even though you're currently deeper inside a nested call).

Without Call Stack, in a large codebase with many files and functions calling each other, you'd have to manually trace back through code reading it top-down trying to guess the execution path. Call Stack just SHOWS you the path directly, live, with zero guessing.

Key takeaway (Lecture 3)

Call Stack = live visual trail of "function A called function B called function C," built using a Last-In-First-Out stack structure (new calls pushed on top, finished calls popped off top). Extremely useful for nested/deep logic where you'd otherwise lose track of "how did I get here." Paired with Step Into (go deeper) and Step Out (come back up), it gives you full control to navigate up and down the execution chain freely during a debug session.

GLOSSARY ADDITION (new terms from this lecture)

Term Meaning
Call Stack The live recorded path of function calls made to reach the current execution point
Stack (data structure) LIFO structure — Last In First Out, like a pile of plates
Push Adding a new frame to the top of the stack (happens when a function is called)
Pop Removing the top frame from the stack (happens when a function finishes/returns)
Frame A single entry in the call stack representing one function's current state (its variables + current line)
Step Out Finishes the current function completely, returns control to the caller (pops current frame)

LECTURE 3 — CHALLENGE 1: The Pass/Fail Bug

The setup (business requirement — read this first, always)

Program calculates a student's average marks. Business rule: if average >= 40 (greater than OR EQUAL to), student passes.

Test data: 5 marks that average out to exactly 40.

The bug observed

Running the program: average correctly shows 40, but final result says FAIL — which is wrong per the business rule (40 should be a PASS since it's "equal to" 40).

Debugging strategy — the RIGHT way to isolate a bug

This is the most important lesson of this video: don't just throw breakpoints everywhere randomly. Think about which part of the code is even suspicious first.

Step 1: Put a breakpoint where the average gets calculated.
Step 2: Step Into the calculate_average() function → confirm the math: yes, average = 40, correctly calculated. This function is innocent — cross it off your suspect list.
Step 3: Since the average itself is correct but the pass/fail RESULT is wrong, the bug must be in the DECISION logic, not the calculation logic. So now step into the is_pass() function.
Step 4: Inside is_pass(), there's only one line: return average > 40.

The actual bug

Code used > (strictly greater than). Business rule needs >= (greater than OR equal to). Since average was EXACTLY 40, average > 40 evaluates to False → wrongly returns fail.

Fix: Change > to >=. Re-run → average 40 → correctly returns Pass.

Key takeaway (Lecture 3)

This bug is a classic off-by-boundary logic error — extremely common in real code (happens with > vs >=, < vs <= constantly). The debugging LESSON here isn't really about VS Code buttons — it's about narrowing down which function is broken by checking outputs at each stage, instead of guessing randomly. If step A's output is correct, don't waste time re-checking step A — move to step B.

LECTURE 4 — CHALLENGE 2: The Shopping Cart Discount Bug

The setup (business requirement)

A shopping cart script calculates total price per item (price × quantity), and applies a discount rule: if an item's subtotal is more than 500, give a 10% discount on that item.

Test data and expected vs actual results

Item Price Qty Subtotal Expected Discount Actual Discount
Keyboard 200 2 400 0 (rule not triggered, ≤500) 0 ✅ correct
Monitor 600 1 600 60 (10% of 600) 30 ❌ wrong
USB Cable 100 1 100 0 0 ✅ correct

Only the Monitor (the item that actually crosses the 500 threshold) is producing a wrong discount. That's your first clue — the bug ONLY shows up when the discount rule is triggered.

Debugging strategy

Step 1: Set breakpoints at calculate_cart_total() (main loop controller) and inside apply_discount() (suspected problem zone, since only discount values are wrong — item totals themselves are fine).

Step 2: Step Into calculate_cart_total(). Watch the cart list itself: cart[1] shows Monitor's price (600) and quantity (1) — confirms raw input data is correct.

Step 3: Loop iteration 1 (Keyboard): item_total correctly computed as 400 (200 × 2). Discount = 0. No issue here — cross this off.

Step 4: Loop iteration 2 (Monitor): item_total correctly computed as 600. Now Step Into apply_discount() specifically because this is where subtotal > 500 becomes true for the first time — this is the exact branch where the bug can hide.

Step 5: Manually verify using Watch panel: 600 * 0.1 = 60 (this is what 10% of 600 SHOULD be, calculated independently as a sanity check).

Step 6: Check what the actual code produces at that same point: discount = 30, not 60.

The actual bug

The code was written with 0.05 (5%) instead of 0.1 (10%) inside the discount formula. A wrong constant/hardcoded value — the logic structure (if subtotal > 500, apply discount) was correct, but the actual PERCENTAGE was wrong.

Fix: Change 0.05 to 0.1. Re-run → Monitor discount = 60, total cart calculation now correct: 400 + 600 + 100 = 1100, minus 60 discount = 1040 final total.

Key takeaway (Lecture 4)

Two separate lessons stack here:

  1. Trace only the branch where the bug shows up. Since Keyboard and USB Cable (both under the 500 threshold) worked fine, there was zero need to debug them — only the Monitor (above threshold) needed investigation.
  2. Manually calculate the expected value using Watch panel, then compare it to what the code actually outputs. This "expected vs actual" comparison technique is how you catch wrong constants/hardcoded numbers hiding inside otherwise-correct-looking logic.
  3. Not every bug needs Watch Panel or Conditional Breakpoints — sometimes plain Step Into/Step Over is enough. Use the simplest tool that solves the problem; don't over-engineer your debugging process.

GLOSSARY — every term used, in one place

Term Meaning
Breakpoint A marker on a line that pauses program execution when reached
Continue Runs code until the next breakpoint
Step Over Runs current line fully, skips inside any function calls, moves to next line
Step Into Enters a function call to inspect its internal execution
Restart Restarts the debug session from scratch
Watch Panel A live, custom panel where you type expressions/variables to monitor continuously
Scope The region of code where a variable is "alive" and accessible. Local variables die (go out of scope) once their function ends
Ternary expression A one-line if-else in Python: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false
Conditional breakpoint (mentioned, covered later) — a breakpoint that only triggers when a specific condition is true, not every time
Virtual environment (venv) An isolated Python environment per project, keeping dependencies separate from global Python
Off-by-boundary bug A bug caused by wrong comparison operator, e.g. using > instead of >=
